title: ChatGPT and the digitisation of writing
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how ChatGPT is affecting students’ writing practices in higher education and situates that change within the broader long-term digitisation of writing. The authors aim to understand how postgraduate students were using ChatGPT and other digital writing tools, what benefits and problems they perceived, and what strengths and weaknesses they showed in what the authors call “generative AI literacy.” The study is not about K-12 reading outcomes and does not provide causal evidence on foundational literacy instruction.

The study examines students’ real-world use of ChatGPT alongside other writing-related digital tools such as Grammarly, Quillbot, Wordtune, DeepL, and Google Translate. The researchers also propose a conceptual framework for generative AI literacy covering pragmatic, safety, reflective, socio-ethical, and contextual understanding. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and observation of participants’ writing processes, then analysed thematically.

Participants were 23 postgraduate taught and postgraduate research students at a British university, with diverse national backgrounds including the UK, China, India, Thailand, Japan, Greece, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, and the USA. All were engaged in academic writing tasks such as essays, dissertations, or theses. The context was one higher education institution in the UK during summer 2023, before the university had issued a formal AI policy.

The main findings were that students used ChatGPT in varied, highly individualised ways, especially for understanding assignment briefs, structuring writing, summarising readings, rephrasing text, and checking grammar. Students valued the tool for efficiency and stress reduction but worried about inaccuracy, plagiarism accusations, and dependence on technology. The authors conclude that ChatGPT has made the digitisation of writing more visible and controversial, creating an opportunity for universities to strengthen students’ generative AI literacy. The paper does not test effectiveness on academic performance and offers no randomized or quasi-experimental evidence.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed qualitative study using semi-structured interviews and observations, but it is not an RCT or quasi-experiment and provides no causal evidence. It is also outside the target population and setting for the retrieval question: higher education writing rather than K-12 foundational reading.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests perceived efficiency gains and mixed perceived impacts on writing and thinking, but impact is unclear because there are no quantitative outcome estimates or causal comparisons. For the K-12 foundational reading question, this study provides only adjacent evidence and should not be interpreted as direct evidence of impact.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT and related digital writing assistants used by postgraduate students to support academic writing tasks such as understanding assignment briefs, summarising readings, structuring essays, paraphrasing, proofreading, and grammar support.
ChatGPT used conversationally as an interactive assistant for explaining concepts, clarifying assignment requirements, brainstorming, and iterative question-answer support during writing.

finding.finding_summary: In qualitative interviews and observations with 23 postgraduate students at a British university, students reported that ChatGPT and other writing tools supported multiple stages of academic writing, including comprehension of assignment briefs, summarisation, structuring, paraphrasing, and proofreading. At the same time, some participants expressed concern that use of ChatGPT could reduce independent thinking, weaken authentic authorial voice, or create overdependence; no standardized literacy assessments, causal comparisons, or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative interview and observational reports of writing practices, perceived benefits, and perceived drawbacks in academic writing

finding.finding_summary: Students described ChatGPT as helping them manage difficult concepts, brainstorm, and break through writing blocks, suggesting perceived support for metacognitive and self-management aspects of writing. However, several participants explicitly worried that the tool 'stopped me from thinking' or reduced motivation to think independently, indicating possible erosion of independent critical thinking; no quantitative measures or effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of independent thinking, reflection, and writing-process support

finding.finding_summary: A prominent theme was that students perceived ChatGPT and related tools as improving efficiency, saving time, and reducing stress during academic writing. These conclusions are based on self-reported perceptions from interviews and observations rather than objective time-on-task or productivity metrics, and no effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported efficiency, time-saving, and stress reduction during writing

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported uncertainty about appropriate use of generative AI and wanted clearer institutional policies and guidance, suggesting that ChatGPT is already influencing university governance around academic integrity and AI literacy. The paper argues that the controversy around generative AI creates an opportunity for institutions to engage students in policy and AI-literacy development, but provides no causal institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of policy uncertainty, perceived need for guidance, and institutional implications
